title: My Claude strategy for building a vertical slice instead of one-shotting a whole game (template + full prompt)
author: Comet7777
selftext:
**Slight PSA** \- showing off one-shotting games is somewhat impressive, but also makes AI game dev look sloppy and unimaginative. The anti-AI crowd don't need more ammunition.   
  
Asking Claude to “make me a Zelda game” works, technically. You get a game, but it’s going to be a VERY generic game: every gap you left gets filled with an assumption that is answered with the most common denominator answer. In Ep. 2 of my series I show the setup I use instead:

* A Game design-doc - so every chat starts from the same source of truth, and Claude keeps the doc updated as decisions change. 
* Step 1 of the prompt: questions only. - “Read the doc. Before writing any code, ask me up to 8 questions that would change how you build the slice, suggest a default answer for each, then stop and wait.”
* Step 2: the scope of a vertical slice to test your assumption - Exactly what to build (one area, one dungeon, one weapon, two enemies, one boss, one ability gate), exactly what NOT to build (XP, inventory, saves, cutscenes), and no external art: shapes are code-generated, so I test fun before spending time on art.
* Delivery rules - a full Godot project zip, not patches, and Claude runs the build and checks for errors before handing it over.

I break it down (in great length, if you're into that) in this video. You can also check out the free game design template in the video description: [https://youtu.be/NNn10FiuZG8](https://youtu.be/NNn10FiuZG8)  
  
The prompt I use is this:

    You're my game development partner on [GAME NAME], a new game I'm building solo with AI tools. You'll handle the code and help with design; I make the creative calls.
    
    The attached game design doc is the source of truth. If something isn't in it, ask before adding it. Keep the doc updated as we make decisions, and log each change in its decision log.
    
    STEP 1: QUESTIONS FIRST
    Read the design doc. Before writing any code, ask me up to 8 questions about anything unclear, contradictory or missing that would change how you build the vertical slice. Group them by topic, put the most important first, and suggest a default answer for each. Then stop and wait for my answers.
    
    STEP 2: BUILD THE VERTICAL SLICE (after I answer)
    Build the smallest playable slice that tests the assumptions in section 9 of the doc:
    - Engine: [ENGINE AND LANGUAGE, e.g. Godot 4, GDScript]. Base resolution [e.g. 480x270], scaled to [e.g. 1920x1080] with pixel-perfect scaling. [TILE SIZE, e.g. 16x16 tiles].
    - [THE PLAYABLE SPACE: e.g. one level, one area and one small dungeon, or one arena].
    - [THE PLAYER: movement and core actions, e.g. 8-direction movement, a melee attack, a dodge, brief invincibility after taking a hit].
    - [ENEMIES: 1 to 2 types, each with one line on its behavior].
    - [THE PAYOFF: e.g. one boss that grants an ability, and one place where that ability opens a new path].
    - Controls: [KEY BINDINGS]. [Controller support too, if needed.]
    - A simple HUD: [e.g. health and the current ability].
    - NO external art or audio files. Draw everything in code with simple shapes and a limited palette ([YOUR PALETTE]). Make the player, each enemy and any boss easy to tell apart by shape and color. Placeholder sound effects are fine if you can generate them in code; otherwise leave them out.
    
    Do NOT build: [YOUR OUT-OF-SCOPE LIST, e.g. XP, skill trees, inventory, shops, saving, dialogue systems, cutscenes], a title screen beyond "press Enter to start," or any area beyond the ones above. If you think something else is needed, suggest it; don't build it.
    
    DELIVERY
    - Send the full project as one zip I can unzip and open in [ENGINE]. No patches.
    - Before handing it over, run the project and check it starts without errors. If you can run it headless, include screenshots of [THE KEY MOMENTS, e.g. the main area, the dungeon and the boss].
    - Give me a short list: what's in the build, how to play it start to finish, anything you weren't sure about, and what you'd test first.

comments.author: HeavyMike
comments.body: why are you so rude to the AI, you don't even say please?

replies.author: Comet7777
replies.body: I’m always saying please and thank you and great job! (Anthropic, don’t ban me)

comments.author: Brief_Shopping2222
comments.body: I've been working on the same game since before AI could write code. It's finally at a point that feels semi-professional and is fun to play against bots. I can't imagine trying to one shot something and brag about it. No less let AI do 95% of the work for you.

replies.author: Frequent-Motor-492
replies.body: The age of the programmer is over. It's sucks but it's the reality. You will get 1% of what everyone else is getting done. But honestly, the hard part was the content. So become a great content builder.

replies.author: Savings-Aioli-2305
replies.body: I have not seen a single good thing made by a vibe coder, but every great game has been made by real progammers.

replies.author: Frequent-Motor-492
replies.body:
Yes AI can create slop. It can also create tight secure well polish products. You still have to put the time in and tell the AI every detail and know what to ask. There are plenty of good games out there that are "vibe coded" but they wouldn't dare tell anyone should the Luddites storm the castle. 
Also this is all brand new. All games made moving forward are being "vibe coded".

replies.author: Savings-Aioli-2305
replies.body: should be interesting in a few years when peoples working knowledge base has decreased so much that they have no idea what the AI is doing. Hopefully some people stay disciplined and not proudly state that programming is over.

replies.author: Frequent-Motor-492
replies.body: That's an interesting point. I hope so too. We put a lot of faith in people who are looking pretty shady these days.

replies.author: Savings-Aioli-2305
replies.body: yeah at the end of the day it will be a grave we dig ourselves. I use chat gpt sometimes if I am stuck, or to help with learning things, but if I didn't know these things and was using one of these advanced AIs that will write a whole game for you I would have absolutely no clue what it is even doing, if it is using the correct techniques how I actually want. I can see the appeal though, just need to focus on myself because seeing people pump out games without knowing much about game development fills me with a lot of existential dread so maybe I am just coping.

replies.author: Comet7777
replies.body: I’m the same way, but everyone is flexing their one shots and I’m just here thinking “bro, that won’t scale at all. So much refactoring ahead of you!”

replies.author: Brief_Shopping2222
replies.body:
I think there is a sort of honeymoon euphoria going on with AI coding right now, especially game dev. I've gone through bouts of it myself, but there always comes a sobering point where you realize that you actually need to understand how games are built and why they are built that way. This isn't so much true with simple flappy frogger clones, but anything with any sort of depth or even multiplayer is going to become an exercise in pain until you do your homework. 

 Another factor is artwork. When the vast majority of people are relying on AI for all their assets, a vast majority of games are going to be identified by that and ignored.

comments.author: OakNLeaf
comments.body: I use this same process. I have a highly detailed GDD and have asked Claude to read through it and ask questions on items that are not clear, never to make assumptions and it's been going pretty well

comments.author: EasyTarget973
comments.body:
best comment I saw recently, anything good is still  in development

nice to see people passing this info on though. 

also most things in this sphere will be free next year. paying for games won't be a thing, I think. it'll be rare.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
lol OP thinks he needs to preach as if nobody else is writing specs like him...

actual PSA: one-prompt experiments are unique to AI development because it is a benchmarking activity.

It is usually very useful for understanding token costs and new AI model capabilities. those one-prompters almost always share their prompts and setups too. It is actually very good resources. 

many devs in this sub fail to grasp this simple idea and they are stuck doing things the old way. I literally have to tell people "hey you don't have to do this or that anymore under the new models" regularly because they tuned out of those one-prompt posts

next time, spend 30 seconds to a minute whenever you see those one-prompt posts. Look at it from the AI tech perspective. 

stop trying to party with the Anti. they will not respect you and honor your effort no matter how much you want to cater to them. They don't want people to use AI period. They have a laundry list of reasons to oppose AI and people like us. 

sorry for the rant

replies.author: Comet7777
replies.body: Just trying to pass on stuff that helped me. Never made the claim that no one else does this - but plenty of proof that others half ass it. You do you.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
the "half-assing" part is normal for solo devs.

many of these solo devs just work quietly on their own without additional inputs from others.

sharing games in subs like this one can be the first time they ever share their game online to anyone.

this is true for ai and manual by the way.

so don't judge quickly unless you already have a game out there is certified not "half-ass" by others.

your game will always look better to you because it is your pet project

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
Most of one shot games are people who want cosplay game developers, or who want to flood the steam with low effort games to make money. I talk here about the games where the prompt could be made by 12 year old    who would probably make a better game with AI.

And it is highly disappointing to see a person who actually wants to share knowledge and experience getting shit.

Like you want this sub be advertisement for AI companies or you want it to be a genuine game dev sub?

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
do you look at those one-prompt game posts much actually? if you do, you do know that some of them are free, right? legit one-prompters share their prompt and their usage data too. 

I also doubt that 12 years are allowed to burn money on tokens. maybe some kids are that rich, no idea

I personally have reviewed over 30 games from this sub so I would say I contribute a bit toward the sub being "a geniune game dev sub"

I also had to routinely reminded people of the latest AI capability on this sub because people get told not to pay attention to those one-prompt posts i.e. someone asked how to deal modular mesh for gear/equipment when we got easy solution since like 2-3 months ago...

seriously, there should be a PSA to remind people to check one-prompt posts whenever a new model drops.

comments.body: “Every gap gets filled with an assumption” should be the number 1 tip for everyone coding with AI should follow.
